title: Was Napoleon Really Short? Autopsy Says 168 cm, So Who Drew Him Small?
description:
May 1821, Saint Helena. The day after Napoleon died, his personal physician, Antommarchi, recorded his height as "5 feet 2 inches 4 lines"; Darling, the English craftsman who handled his funeral, measured him with an English ruler at "5 feet 7 inches." One man, two numbers.

This episode goes in order: the "Little Corporal" of 1796, Gillray's "Little Boney" of 1803, the minimum height of the Guard grenadiers, the thousand-plus small boats off Plymouth in 1815, and then back to 1821: the old French foot was longer than the English one, so 5 feet 2 inches 4 lines is about 168 to 169 cm, taller than the average Frenchman of the time. Last comes the earliest "Napoleon complex," in an American newspaper in 1923.

"Read with an English ruler, it's only 157 cm" is this channel's arithmetic; no source records anyone reading it that way at the time, and the sources don't say directly which foot the autopsy used. Sentences that begin "We think" are this channel's view.

The illustrations in this episode are AI-generated; the historical figures are cartoon characters, unnamed and not meant to resemble anyone.

Information as of 2026-10-19 (rewritten 2026-10-25 under new rules)

nb001.text: You've surely heard it: Napoleon was short.

nb002.text: So short that, for 100 years, English has named quarrelsome short men after him.

nb003.text: May 1821. Saint Helena, in the South Atlantic.

nb004.text: The day after he died, a doctor measured his height with a ruler.

nb006.text: But the English craftsman at his funeral, with an English ruler, got 5 feet 7 inches.

nb008.text: That's not the strangest part. While he lived, London print shops hung a little man stamping his foot.

nb009.text: The summer of his defeat, over a thousand boats rowed to a British warship just to see him.

nb010.text: This file follows 5 feet 2 inches for 200 years, to today's dictionary.

nb011.text: So how tall was Napoleon? And where did "short" come from?

nb101.text: "Little" stuck to him 25 years before the doctor's ruler, and at first, it wasn't about height.

nb102.text: In 1796, at 26, he was leading an army in Italy.

nb103.text: He had to take the wooden bridge at Lodi, nearly 200 meters long, with 30 Austrian guns on the far bank.

nb104.text: His troops charged across under fire.

nb105.text: As a veteran who just charged across behind a 26-year-old general, what would you call him?

nb106.text: Las Cases, his companion on the island, wrote:

nb107.text: After each battle, veterans gathered to "promote" the young general one rank.

nb108.text: After Lodi, they "made" him corporal, and "the Little Corporal" spread through the ranks.

nb110.text: In French, "little" can also be affectionate, like calling a buddy "little Joe."

nb111.text: Corporal is a very low rank; the usual view is the veterans took the general as one of their own.

nb112.text: But honestly, this "promotion" story isn't in the records of the time; only Las Cases tells it.

nb113.text: His reason: "his youth, or something else." Not one word about height.

nb114.text: But those who drew him short were mostly across the Channel.

nb115.text: There, calling him "little" meant something else entirely. And did he care?

nb201.text: He did. In 1802, France formally asked Britain to rein in the papers attacking him.

nb202.text: The next May, the two nations were at war again.

nb203.text: That year, London print-shop windows often displayed him.

nb204.text: A hugely popular London cartoonist, Gillray, made nearly 1,000 satires in his life.

nb206.text: No. He never once met Napoleon in person.

nb207.text: Remember the stamping little man? Gillray drew him.

nb208.text: That May's print: he jumps in rage, shakes his fists, and shouts.

nb209.text: His hat with its big plume lies on the floor.

nb210.text: In the prints he's always much shorter than everyone, yet his hat is huge.

nb211.text: Titles call him "Little Boney." In 1803 alone, at least 5 had it in the title.

nb212.text: If you were a Londoner then, passing that window, would you stop and laugh?

nb213.text: Another goes further: Britain's king holds him in his palm, eyes him by spyglass, calls him an odious little reptile.

nb214.text: The first time I saw that king's-palm print, my first reaction was: that's brutal.

nb215.text: By August, other artists' prints joined in, calling him "the little Corsican."

nb216.text: The next year, he became emperor. This time, the cartoons got help from the men at his side.

nb301.text: Beside the emperor stood his Guard, the grenadiers.

nb302.text: Guard grenadiers had a minimum height. How tall?

nb303.text: An 1802 order set it at 5 feet 6 inches, roughly 178 centimeters.

nb304.text: Later orders eased it a little, still around 176 centimeters.

nb305.text: Far taller than most; just think, what did 178 centimeters mean 200 years ago?

nb306.text: Add tall bearskin caps, and they flank him on both sides.

nb307.text: An ordinary-height man in a row of tall men looks a size smaller.

nb308.text: He often wore a plain grey coat and an unplumed hat; among gold-braided officers, he stood out most.

nb309.text: Easiest to spot, and I'd guess to draw. The result?

nb310.text: In February 1805, Gillray drew another: he and Britain's prime minister carve a globe-shaped pudding.

nb311.text: The prime minister is tall and thin; he's short and stocky, rising from his chair to reach it.

nb312.text: When I saw that pudding, I laughed out loud.

nb313.text: In 1807, Gillray drew another, titling him "the little Corsican gardener."

nb314.text: For over a decade of war, British cartoons drew him this way.

nb315.text: Did Britons ever get to see how small "Little Boney" really was?

nb316.text: They did, and thousands came at once.

nb401.text: That was 1815. In June, Napoleon lost at Waterloo.

nb402.text: Gillray missed this day: he died in early June that year; Waterloo was June 18.

nb403.text: It got to me a little: after drawing him all those years, he missed his fall by just over two weeks. Did the pens drawing him stop?

nb404.text: No. Another cartoonist, Cruikshank, kept drawing him small.

nb405.text: One the year before, one after the surrender: both titles still say "Little Boney."

nb406.text: Remember those thousand boats? It was that very summer.

nb407.text: The defeated Napoleon was held aboard a British warship off Plymouth.

nb408.text: Thousands of Britons rowed out; the captain reckoned no fewer than 8 per boat on average.

nb409.text: Just think: after years of cartoons, they finally saw the real man. What did they see?

nb410.text: The British captain later wrote: he was sturdy, about 5 feet 7 inches tall.

nb411.text: This time he was alive, on deck; the measurer changed, the number didn't.

nb412.text: And the doctor's 5 feet 2 inches? Six years later, on the island.

nb501.text: The doctor who measured him was his own physician, and he used a French ruler.

nb502.text: What he wrote was even more precise: 5 feet 2 inches, plus 4 lines.

nb503.text: An inch had 12 lines; 4 lines is a third of an inch.

nb504.text: Here's the catch: the French foot and the English foot weren't the same length.

nb505.text: An old French foot was about 32.5 centimeters; an English foot, just 30.5.

nb506.text: Same with the inch: the French one was a bit longer.

nb507.text: By the old French measure, that's about 168 or 169 centimeters.

nb509.text: Converted from English units, around 170 centimeters.

nb510.text: Same man, two rulers, nearly the same in centimeters. The two numbers from the start match up.

nb511.text: And Napoleon's own government's papers put "5 feet 2 inches" at 1.678 meters.

nb512.text: His valet's memoir gives 5 feet 2 inches 3 lines, just one line off the doctor's.

nb513.text: Another attendant's memoir gives exactly the doctor's figure.

nb514.text: But what if someone read the doctor's number with an English ruler?

nb515.text: Then it's only 157 centimeters. The two readings differ by 11 centimeters.

nb516.text: To be clear: no source says "someone misread it this way"; this is our own arithmetic.

nb517.text: There's a third reading, too: by the everyday foot after 1812, he'd be 4 centimeters taller.

nb518.text: France had had the meter for over 20 years; had the doctor used it, we wouldn't be guessing.

nb519.text: Was that height short for the time?

nb520.text: Scholars estimate adult French men then averaged about 164 or 165 centimeters.

nb521.text: The average comes from Napoleonic conscription, measuring recruits around age 20.

nb522.text: He was a few centimeters above that average.

nb523.text: You might say: that's not tall, is it?

nb524.text: True, next to today's average Taiwanese man, he isn't tall; but his peers were the people of his time.

nb526.text: Remember the stamping little man in the window? That reading fits him exactly.

nb527.text: To English speakers, he thus became a little man.

nb528.text: And 100 years later, the little man would get a formal name.

nb601.text: Remember that 100-year-old word from the opening? The earliest found is in a 1923 American paper.

nb602.text: A Washington daily said a man had a "Napoleon complex": he thought himself great.

nb603.text: Then it meant arrogance, nothing to do with height.

nb605.text: Merriam-Webster says today's meaning first appeared in 1924.

nb606.text: It's often explained with Viennese psychologist Adler's theory.

nb607.text: Adler said people try to make up for where they feel inferior.

nb608.text: So did Adler coin the name?

nb609.text: No sign of it. His own books mention Napoleon, but for hero worship, not height.

nb610.text: Yet the word grew into today's sense: short, and so extra competitive and quarrelsome.

nb611.text: Today, Merriam-Webster defines it this way: a domineering or aggressive attitude, seen as making up for being small.

nb614.text: Oxford Learner's and Cambridge don't have this entry.

nb615.text: Napoleon himself never heard the term. When he died, Adler wasn't even born.

nb616.text: Are short men really more combative?

nb617.text: A 2007 study at a British university said: no.

nb618.text: A 2018 Dutch experiment found short men facing taller ones were no quicker to lash out.

nb619.text: But when they decided the split, they kept a bit more.

nb620.text: But whatever the experiments say, you still hear people say it today: oh, him? Napoleon complex.

nb621.text: We think the name stuck so easily thanks to the century-plus of cartoons before it.

nb623.text: The 5 feet 2 inches he recorded was never short at all.

nb625.text: Where'd you first hear Napoleon was short? Tell me below.

nb626.text: This channel sticks to what's on record; subscribe to open the files with us.
